description: We are freshmen in 9th grade who love to code and design apps that help people and make a real impact on the world.
summary: We developed Outpost Academy, an interactive lunar mission that offers hands-on mission and real space science while keeping it interactive and fun for people of any age, especially those aged 7-12. Addressing the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, players activate an outpost, produce oxygen by rearranging water molecules, repair habitat leaks, manage power, grow plants, and drive a rover to collect samples across three craters, unlocking an extra Mars mission. A standout feature of our project is our connection to NASA's DONKI space-weather database: fresh solar-particle and eligible solar-flare notifications trigger simulated emergencies, challenging players to reach shelter or protect the outpost's power systems. Real observations inspire these events, while their gameplay consequences are simplified educational models. Every mission connects scientific understanding with decisions about oxygen, energy, and cargo. Adjustable Mission Control guidance, read-aloud support, assisted driving, and shared-screen teamwork make learning more accessible to kids. Debriefs and "what-if" comparisons help players understand their choices, building STEM curiosity, problem-solving skills, and the challenges of living beyond Earth.
details:
Outpost Academy - First Footprints is an interactive, browser-based mission trainer designed to help children ages 7–12 explore the science and teamwork behind space exploration. Players become junior astronauts responsible for activating a lunar outpost, keeping its systems working, and completing rover expeditions across three craters. Completing the lunar campaign unlocks a Mars bonus exercise.

How it works

Players learn by operating equipment and making decisions. In the oxygen lab, they break water’s chemical bonds and rearrange the conserved atoms into hydrogen and oxygen. Other activities involve repairing a habitat seal, connecting electrical circuits, allocating limited power, and supplying a greenhouse with water and light. Before each rover expedition, players choose a route and balance supplies, tools, and sample storage. They then drive through terrain, respond to field advisories, and collect, label, and secure samples.

A distinctive feature is the connection to NASA’s DONKI space-weather database. The game checks NASA notifications, and fresh solar-particle or eligible solar-flare reports can trigger modeled emergencies. Players must reach the habitat and operate protective systems or safeguard the outpost’s power supply. Notifications include timestamps and source links; older records are distinguished from current alerts. Practice drills remain available when no live event is occurring. The emergency timers and consequences are educational game mechanics, not actual lunar hazard forecasts.

Benefits and intended impact

Our goal is to make STEM concepts tangible, engaging, and approachable. Players see how chemistry, engineering, resource management, and exploration depend on one another. Mission debriefs and “what if” comparisons encourage reflection, helping players understand how different choices change outcomes. Shared-screen pilot and Mission Control roles also encourage communication and teamwork.

Tools and development

We developed the game using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Canvas-based artwork and animation. A small server connects to NASA’s data while keeping the API key out of the browser. Progress saves locally, and the project is hosted through ChatGPT Sites. ChatGPT/Codex assisted with coding, interface text, debugging, and testing. The in-game Mission Control companion uses scripted, state-aware guidance.

Creativity and design considerations

Our creative approach connects hands-on science activities to an ongoing adventure: producing oxygen and repairing equipment directly support later exploration. Real NASA observations bring events beyond the game into the experience.

We considered scientific accuracy, age-appropriate complexity, accessibility, and opportunities to learn from mistakes. Adjustable guidance, read-aloud support, larger text, reduced motion, keyboard-accessible controls, and assisted driving support different learners. Ordinary resource costs follow chosen actions, allowing time to read and think. NASA references and explanations identify where the simulation simplifies reality, helping players connect enjoyable gameplay with credible science
